It came to the surface nearly a year later, following a bench-clearing brawl with the New York Yankees on Thursday afternoon, as the Detroit Tigers’ frustration finally festered to the point of in-fighting.
The Tigers’ private discontent with Victor Martinez is now public.

In the bottom of the seventh inning, television cameras caught Martinez in an animated-enough exchange with right-hander Justin Verlander before advancing toward him and being held back by third baseman Nick Castellanos.

Moved this graf up: Neither Martinez nor Verlander have spoken about Thursday’s exchange, but it likely was initiated because Martinez played peacemaker during the on-field fracas in the seventh inning with Yankees catcher Gary Sanchez – who threw punches at both Castellanos and first baseman Miguel Cabrera in the sixth inning – and righty reliever Dellin Betances, who had just hit catcher James McCann in the head with a fastball.
And this one: About the exchange, Castellanos told the Free Press, “We handled it. It’s an in-house matter and it’s been handled.”
And this one: But what hasn’t been handled is the big problem that Martinez has become.

The exchange pitted a pair of veteran players who are publicly thought of as team leaders. It also illuminated the reality that for the past two seasons, it has become clear within the Tigers clubhouse that Martinez, the 38-year-old designated hitter, is far from a leader. In fact, the picture painted by people within the organization – from players to coaches to front office figures – is one of an entitled player who isn’t a positive influence and presents a problem for the team going forward. <<>>>

This season, Martinez’s offensive production has declined in earnest. He is hitting .253 with 10 home runs and 47 RBIs. He is a liability on the basepaths with no position in the field. Next season, he is owed $18 million in the final year of a four-year deal signed prior to the 2014 season.

Martinez’s exchange with Verlander comes almost a year to the date of his boorish behavior reaching a breaking point in the clubhouse, which came in the aftermath of an Aug. 27 loss to the Angels last season. In that game, four Tigers were ejected for arguing balls and strikes, including Martinez.

According to multiple persons with knowledge of the situation who requested anonymity because they are not authorized to speak on clubhouse matters, when the team entered the clubhouse after that game, Martinez was nowhere to be seen. He had left Comerica Park early.
Asked if an ejected player leaving the stadium was commonplace, one former teammate said, “I had never seen it before in my life.”

The early departure was a talking point inside the clubhouse. Those words filtered back to Martinez, who singled out a teammate, confronting him in an incident that never escalated to a physical level, though the players were separated.

Such episodes are not uncommon in clubhouses around baseball: They are the natural byproduct of competitive, testosterone-filled men spending eight months together. Even on winning teams, problems arise.

Though the incident did not seem to have an effect on the team’s play – the Tigers went 17-15 the rest of the way, falling 2 ½ games short of the second American League Wild Card spot – it is considered the point when a silenced Martinez started to detach himself from any sort of leadership role and the team concept itself.
“It’s all about him,” one teammate said. “Non-existent,” is how another described Martinez’s contributions these days.

The majority of the clubhouse supported the teammate’s opinion on Martinez leaving early, including confidantes Miguel Cabrera and Francisco Rodriguez, and the manner in which he responded to the criticism – preferring to puff his chest out and escalate the situation instead of accepting blame for his actions – did not sit well with the group.

Martinez has been the  toughest player for manager Brad Ausmus to manage and a central figure in the Tigers’ clubhouse issues, according to people with knowledge of the situation: Though he is a non-factor on the field – performing below replacement-level standards – the ever-prideful Martinez still clings to his veteran stature. He resisted being moved out of the clean-up spot earlier this season and has reluctantly hit lower in the lineup since returning from the 10-day disabled list with an irregular heartbeat in late June.

It’s a problem Ausmus has not solved and one the front office has shown no desire to solve by simply releasing him,<<<<<<>>>> though the topic has been raised from the coaching staff. Martinez has roughly $21 million remaining on his contract. <<>>>

He has spoken in the past about his retirement plans. He said in the spring he would like to finish his contract, and in June he said: “When the day comes and I can’t really play well, I don’t think about that. I know when I’m going to play. If I can’t play before that, it’s all in God’s hands, not my hands.”

The day of Martinez not playing well has come. That, in itself, was inevitable. The Tigers knew as much when late owner Mike Ilitch made Martinez’s re-signing a priority, even if it meant committing big money years after the team projected he would remain productive.
But the solution to the problem is in Martinez’s hands.

He can choose to continue on the path he’s traveled for the past year, unable to come to grips with his declining skills and unwilling to take a reduced role, represented in the Tigers’ clubhouse only as a “very distracting” ion of bad energy, as one coach said.
Or he can forge a new path, realistic of his ability, reverting to his team-first form of the past and serve as a sounding board for the young players who make up a substantial part of the clubhouse.

A tiger cannot change its stripes. And if Martinez, the eldest Tiger, decides he can’t, either, then perhaps he should think about Ilitch, the man who made him so handsomely rich into his late 30s, not only for his production but also his presence.
“He’s a special guy,” Ilitch said at the time of his re-signing. “His teammates think the world of him, so he’s a special person, I’d say.”

And if Victor Martinez decides he can’t be that person any longer, then maybe he should do the honorable thing and hand over next season’s salary, getting a head start on his central Florida cattle ranch, far from the Tigers clubhouse where he is much more of a problem than a solution these days.
Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press
Tigers beat writer
Twitter: @anthonyfenech
